children.body:
I agree. “Dying” means something is going down to zero and, once there, will stay at zero. That is almost certainly not happening to the humanities.

The proper word here is “declining”. The humanities are on a downswing right now but people still want them. We still need people to teach history and literature, make good art, lead us and inspire us. Those needs are not going away. As long as there are humans there will be humanities.

comments.body: The collapse in new humanities PhDs is a good thing. It is unfair to students to admit them to programs where their chance of getting a tenure track position is one in a thousand. They end up spending the prime years of their lives pulling out their hair in order to become less employable. I question the judgment of the tenured professors who made this decision way back in the nineties. It seems profoundly selfish to me. The class size of the top twenty programs should be commensurate to the actual supply of jobs.

comments.body:
2. The graph you have for investment is only for the "construction" component of investment, the buildings and powerlines, which are only a small part of AI investment since it won't include the GPUs, racks, gas turbines, etc. This should be obvious because the orders of magnitude are off. US AI investment in 2026 isn't 50 billion; it's more like 500 billion. Alex Tabarrok's post quotes another graph from Krugman with his estimate of all tech vs non-tech investment, which looks much more convincing.

But ultimately any story about "crowding out" relies on what counterfactual you select. This is the gist of the disagreement between Tabarrok and Krugman, and your timing argument against. Instead of asking if there's crowding out or not, instead just ask if in another world where there weren't 500-1000 billion of AI investment in one year alone, whether interest rates would be higher or lower. That's the key question. I think the answer is non-trivial, but I tend toward higher.

comments.body:
It’s not just social media - it’s also games and short-form video apps on smartphones.

All three of these are addictionware, designed to suck people in and keep them hooked. I don’t know how many smartphone games you’ve played but most of them are amazingly bad, designed to addict you and make you feel compelled to spend a certain time every day playing.

It was hard to kick my addictions to those games, but I managed to do it and I’ve stayed away since. I learned a lesson: be the boss of your phone, don’t let it be the boss of you!
